Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• 26-year-old man with known asthma ran out of controller (beclomethasone) and reliever (salbutamol) inhalers 1 week ago.  
• Presents with 3 h history of chest tightness, mild exertional shortness of breath, wheeze, and non-productive cough following recent viral URI.  
• No chest pain, hemoptysis, fever, or resting dyspnea. Able to speak full sentences.

Working diagnosis  
Acute asthma exacerbation precipitated by viral upper-respiratory infection and lapse in inhaled therapy (supported by DDx highest-likelihood item).

Considerations  
• Viral acute bronchitis with reactive airways (medium likelihood) – overlaps clinically; monitor for progression.  
• Community-acquired pneumonia or pulmonary embolism considered low likelihood given absence of fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, or risk factors.

Management  
• Prescribed salbutamol inhaler (SABA) and beclomethasone inhaler (ICS) with instructions to resume regular use (Clenil daily, Ventolin PRN).  
• 5-day course oral corticosteroid (2 tablets each morning) provided to reduce airway inflammation.  
• Spacer supplied with education on correct technique.  
• Safety-net advice: seek medical attention if Ventolin required more frequently than every 3 h, or if worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, or light-headedness.  
• Sick leave advised until symptom improvement.  
• No immediate investigations ordered; patient stable at rest during telehealth review.

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification:  Discussed importance of medication adherence, correct spacer technique, and early presentation if symptoms escalate.  
- Patient health goals and priorities:  Patient wishes to avoid severe exacerbation/intubation; priority to obtain inhalers quickly.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Acute asthma exacerbation – High likelihood: known asthma, trigger (viral URI), medication lapse, classic wheeze/tightness.  
2. Viral acute bronchitis with reactive airways – Medium likelihood: persistent post-viral cough and wheeze could contribute.  
3. Community-acquired pneumonia – Low likelihood: post-viral course but absent fever, sputum, or systemic signs.
